title: Sustainer of all

cards: Split a rock in a field, and sometimes there's a tiny creature living inside: a beetle in a damp hollow, a grub, a pale little worm. Nobody brings it groceries. Nobody checks on it.
And yet there it is, alive, with what it needs.
Guru Arjan, the same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, used exactly that picture in a hymn Sikhs recite every evening, and it's the picture under today's line from the twenty-second ashtpadi.

teach.h: RIJAK: WHAT KEEPS A CREATURE ALIVE.
teach.b: The twenty-second ashtpadi, which began by naming God the Master of all beings, says that God sustains each one of them.

The word Sikhs often use for that sustenance is rijak: daily bread, livelihood, what keeps a creature alive. Guru Arjan unfolds the idea in a hymn in raag Gujri that's part of Rehras, the evening prayer.
In paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when God Himself is busy caring for you?

teach.h: IN ROCKS AND STONES, FOOD SET OUT.
teach.b: Even in rocks and stones He made creatures, and set their food before them. Then a second picture.

teach.h: THE CRANE FLIES; THE CHICKS ARE FED.
teach.b: A migrating crane flies hundreds of kos, the old measure of distance, leaving her young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to eat?
Have you never thought of that? The chicks alone, the mother far away, and still they're fed. Now, what this teaching isn't.

teach.h: NOT A REASON TO STOP WORKING.
teach.b: It isn't a promise that no one will ever go hungry, and it isn't permission to stop working.
Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work, and langar feeds whoever comes, because people do go hungry; Sikhs see feeding them as God's work done through human hands. The point is about worry.

Guru Arjan isn't telling the mind to stop trying. He's telling it to stop scheming and fretting as if everything depended on it alone. And often, Sikhs would say, the way God feeds someone is through you.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib hear that God sustains every creature, and each evening in Rehras recite Guru Arjan's hymn picturing food set out even for creatures within rocks.

o: wealth saved up for the hard years
a reward God gives for good prayers
daily bread, what keeps a creature alive

games.q: sustainer of all — tap the pairs.
p: flies far; her chicks are fed

s: Guru Arjan's hymn means Sikhs don't need to work
Sikhs are taught kirat karni, honest work; the hymn is about worry, not effort.
the hymn says God set food before creatures even inside rocks
a picture Sikhs recite every evening in Rehras.
the hymn promises that no one will ever go hungry
it's about worry, not a promise; langar feeds people because people do go hungry.

games.q: the crane has flown hundreds of kos, leaving her chicks. what does Guru Arjan's hymn say?
o: they're fed: who teaches them to eat? God cares for them.
games.why: the hymn asks who feeds them and teaches them to eat, and answers that God is caring for them, so why should the mind scheme and worry?

practice: If you have a pet, give it a little food or fresh water now, slowly; if not, put a few crumbs on a windowsill or water a plant, then sit and breathe.
Watch, or picture, the creature receiving it, and notice that for this moment you're part of how it's sustained. If you pray, say Waheguru as you give.

wordCard.voice: Rijak, sustenance or livelihood: Sukhmani says God sustains each creature with its rijak; Guru Arjan pictures food set out even in rocks, and a crane's chicks fed while she's far away.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rijak, sustenance or livelihood, from the Persian-Arabic rizq.

carryVoice: Your line: he feeds all. The worry can loosen its grip. Day five hundred twenty-four counts.
